2 industrials stocks to consider right now and 1 we avoid

Industrials businesses quietly power the physical things we depend on, from cars and homes to e-commerce infrastructure. Still, their generally high capital requirements expose them to the ups and downs of economic cycles, and the market seems to be baking in a prolonged downturn as the industry has shed 11.7% over the past six months. This drop is a far cry from the S&P 500's 9.1% ascent.

Only some companies are subject to these dynamics, however, and a handful of high-quality businesses can deliver earnings growth in any environment. Taking that into account, here are two industrials stocks we think can generate sustainable market-beating returns and one we would avoid.

One industrials stock to sell:
ChargePoint (CHPT)

Market Cap: $220.4 million

The most prominent EV charging company during the COVID bull market, ChargePoint (NYSE:CHPT) is a provider of electric vehicle charging technology solutions in North America and Europe.

Why Are We Hesitant About CHPT?

Products and services are facing significant end-market challenges during this cycle as sales have declined by 1% annually over the last two years

Negative free cash flow raises questions about the return timeline for its investments

Short cash runway increases the probability of a capital raise that dilutes existing shareholders

At $8.20 per share, ChargePoint trades at 0.5x forward price-to-sales. Check out our free in-depth research report to learn more about why CHPT doesn't pass our bar.

Two industrials stocks to watch:
Lincoln Electric (LECO)

Market Cap: $14.34 billion

Headquartered in Ohio, Lincoln Electric (NASDAQ:LECO) manufactures and sells welding equipment for various industries.

Why Does LECO Catch Our Eye?

Excellent operating margin of 16.5% highlights the efficiency of its business model, and its operating leverage amplified its profits over the last five years

Free cash flow margin grew by 3.9 percentage points over the last five years, giving the company more chips to play with

ROIC punches in at 26.3%, illustrating management's expertise in identifying profitable investments

Lincoln Electric is trading at $256.35 per share, or 22.1x forward P/E. Is now the time to initiate a position? See for yourself in our full research report, it's free.

First Solar (FSLR)

Market Cap: $18.79 billion

Headquartered in Arizona, First Solar (NASDAQ:FSLR) specializes in manufacturing solar panels and providing photovoltaic solar energy solutions.

Why Will FSLR Beat the Market?

Market share has increased this cycle as its 19.5% annual revenue growth over the last two years was exceptional

Free cash flow turned positive over the last five years, showing the company has crossed a key inflection point

Returns on capital are climbing as management makes more lucrative bets

3 software stocks with competitive advantages

Software is rapidly reducing operating expenses for businesses. This secular theme has materialized in superior earnings growth and stock price performance for most SaaS companies, and over the last six months, the industry's 54.6% return has topped the S&P 500 by 45.5 percentage points.

However, only a handful of companies will ultimately thrive over the long term as the low barriers to entry for software businesses lead to fierce competition. With that said, here are three resilient software stocks at the top of our wish list.

JFrog (FROG)

Market Cap: $11.58 billion

Named after the amphibian that continuously evolves from egg to tadpole to adult, JFrog (NASDAQ:FROG) provides a platform that helps organizations securely create, store, manage, and distribute software packages across any system.

Why Are We Bullish on FROG?

Billings growth has averaged 31.5% over the last year, indicating a healthy pipeline of new contracts that should drive future revenue increases

Fast payback periods on sales and marketing expenses allow the company to invest heavily and onboard many customers concurrently

Robust free cash flow margin of 28.3% gives it many options for capital deployment

At $93.19 per share, JFrog trades at 16.7x forward price-to-sales. Is now the time to initiate a position? Find out in our full research report, it's free.

Cadence Design Systems (CDNS)

Market Cap: $89.8 billion

Powering the chips behind everything from smartphones to AI accelerators for over 35 years, Cadence Design Systems (NASDAQ:CDNS) provides essential computational software, hardware, and intellectual property used by engineers to design and verify advanced electronic systems and semiconductors.

Why Could CDNS Be a Winner?

Average billings growth of 17.9% over the last year enhances its liquidity and shows there is steady demand for its products

Superior software functionality and low servicing costs are reflected in its best-in-class gross margin of 86.8%

Software platform has product-market fit given the rapid recovery of its customer acquisition costs

Cadence Design Systems's stock price of $308.58 implies a valuation ratio of 13.4x forward price-to-sales. Is now the right time to buy? See for yourself in our in-depth research report, it's free.

CLEAR Secure (YOU)

Market Cap: $4.69 billion

(Updates with index/price moves, macroeconomic data, and company/geopolitical news from the first paragraph.)

US equity indexes traded mixed as escalating geopolitical tensions and rising energy prices weighed on risk appetite, partially offsetting small gains in technology.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1.2% to 52,255.1, and the S&P 500 declined 0.4% to 7,631.2 after midday Friday. The Nasdaq Composite was less than 0.1% higher at 25,988.3.

All but two sectors declined, led by consumer staples. Energy and technology were the only sectors to rise.

Fifteen of the 20 top-performing stocks in a category with a market capitalization exceeding $200 billion each were from technology, according to data compiled by Finviz. This tech outperformance represents a recovery, as Meta Platforms' (META) plans announced Thursday to increase capital expenditure by $5 billion at the bottom end of the range for 2026 and launch a new, non-voting share class to raise funds helped spark a sell-off in the so-called AI trade.

"Investors continued to assess the recent selloff in AI-related stocks, driven by concerns over the sector's substantial capital requirements," D.A. Davidson said in a research note. "Although the pace of the decline in technology stocks moderated, escalating geopolitical tensions and rising energy prices kept risk appetite subdued."

Saudi Aramco has ordered the evacuation of its headquarters in Dhahran on the Gulf near Bahrain, Reuters reported, as fighting intensified with the Iran-aligned Houthis, Reuters reported. Meanwhile, an oil spill from a tanker was detected off the coast of Umm Al Quwain in the United Arab Emirates, the UAE Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said, according to the news report, without identifying the cause of the spill or the tanker involved.

The front-month West Texas Intermediate crude oil contract jumped 3.8% to $103.29 per barrel, and global benchmark Brent advanced 3.1% to $116.62 per barrel.

"Iranian attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, Houthi attacks on the Saudis, Iran's threats to escalate the means of retaliation, and [President Donald] Trump's post about a week ago to 'finish the job' are all contributing to this sentiment," Derek Holt, head of capital market economics at Scotiabank, said in a note.

The rise in crude prices is adding to inflation concerns and reinforcing expectations that interest rates could remain elevated for longer, the D.A. Davidson note said.

US Treasury yields jumped in midday trading. The 10-year yield climbed 3.1 basis points to 4.98%, the 30-year rate advanced 2.4 basis points to 5.31%, and the two-year yield rose 5.1 basis points to 4.67%.

S&P Global's October flash reading of manufacturing conditions rose to 56.0 from 55.9 in September, versus the 55.5 forecast in a Bloomberg-compiled survey, indicating an expansion to a 53-month high.

The final reading in the University of Michigan consumer sentiment index for October stood at 48.0 from the 46.3 preliminary estimate, beating expectations for no revision in a Bloomberg-compiled poll. That print was below the 48.1 final reported in September. Respondents expected a 4.7% inflation rate over the next year and 3.5% annual inflation over the next five years, both up from 4.6% and 3.4%, respectively, in September.

Gold futures fell 1.3% to $4,008.20, and silver futures dropped 1.8% to $54.02.

Wall Street's benchmark equity indexes were lower intraday as fears of a re-escalation in the Middle East conflict sent US crude oil prices soaring past $100 a barrel again.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.2% at 52,238.5 after midday Friday, while the S&P 500 fell 0.4% to 7,629.7. The Nasdaq Composite edged down 0.1% to 25,984. Except energy and technology, all sectors were in the red, led by consumer staples.

West Texas Intermediate crude oil, the US standard, was up 3.6% at $103.08 a barrel intraday, while Brent jumped 2.9% to $116.46. Brent is on track for the five consecutive weekly gain.

Iran's military is fully prepared for "asymmetric warfare," state-affiliated Tasnim News Agency reported Thursday, citing the nation's army chief.

The report comes as the US and Israel have drawn up specific plans to resume military operations against Iran after the midterm elections in November, The New York Times reported Wednesday, citing sources.

"Markets are increasingly worried about renewed escalation in the Persian Gulf, a scenario that could threaten oil flows that have so far remained remarkably resilient," ING Bank said in Friday report.

Elsewhere in the Middle East, Iran-aligned Houthi rebels have continued to strike Saudi Arabia, CNBC reported.

"Brent has climbed above $114 per barrel and is heading for its highest weekly close since June 2022 as attacks on Saudi Arabian infrastructure raise fears of wider Middle East supply disruptions," Saxo Bank said in Friday report.

Treasury yields were higher intraday, with the 10-year rate up 3.7 basis points at 4.99% and the two-year rate rising 5.1 basis points to 4.67%.

In economic news, US consumer sentiment dropped to its lowest level in five months in October as inflation expectations hit the highest since May, final results of a University of Michigan survey showed.

US private-sector growth eased in October, while employment increased and selling prices rose at the sharpest rate since August 2022, S&P Global's (SPGI) flash purchasing managers' index showed Friday.

In company news, American Express (AXP) reported third-quarter revenue just below Wall Street's expectations, while the payments company's chief executive disclosed plans to terminate about 5% of its global workforce. The stock was down 3.9% intraday, the worst performer on the Dow.

SLB (SLB) reported better-than-expected third-quarter results as a surge in North America revenue and momentum in its data center business offset Middle East headwinds. The oilfield services company's shares jumped 6.7%, the second-biggest gain on the S&P 500.

Deckers Outdoor (DECK) slumped 5.5%. Truist Securities said the footwear designer and distributor's sales guidance cut amid an increasingly promotional US marketplace has fueled growth durability concerns.

Spot gold dipped 0.8% to $3,994.78 per troy ounce, while silver lost 1.7% to $54.05.

Athletic apparel is taking the hardest hit in a retail selloff that's spreading well past any single brand, with premium and performance names sliding at more than twice the pace of the broader sector. Shares of Lululemon Athletica (NASDAQ:LULU) fell 4% to $100.35, extending a 2026 slide that has already erased more than half of the stock's value.

courtesy of Lululemon Athletica

Meanwhile, Under Armour (NYSE:UAA) shares are down 4% to $4.68. Under Armour stock trades far below Lululemon's share price. Yet, the percentage hit is nearly identical, a sign the selling is landing across the whole athletic apparel group.

The SPDR S&P Retail ETF (NYSEARCA:XRT) is down 2% to $87.55, a smaller decline that still shows the pressure reaching well beyond athletic apparel. Broader indexes are holding up better, as the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) is down 0.4% to $760.81.

Selling Spreads Across Discretionary Retail

Lululemon and Under Armour shares are falling harder than the sector fund, and neither has issued a fresh announcement, so the pressure traces to the broader group. Fellow athletic brand Nike (NYSE:NKE) competes for the same active-lifestyle shoppers, keeping the wider footwear and apparel group tied to consumer spending questions. NKE shares are down 2% to $37.54.

Spending data offers a contrast: U.S. retail sales rose 0.8% in September to $745 billion. That strength leaves the selloff driven by sentiment toward premium apparel, where shoppers can easily delay purchases.

Nike (NKE) stock lost 42.1% over the past year, including dividends, compared with a 15.1% gain for the S&P 500. Even after that decline, Nike investors pay more for each dollar of earnings than shareholders of most apparel companies in its peer group. At the same time, Nike's sales growth and profit margin trail nearly all of them. How wide is the gap between what you pay for Nike and what the business delivers?

Nike Costs More Than Tapestry Yet Grows Slower

Nike's price against its earnings is the second highest among the four companies in its group with a comparable figure, while its sales growth and operating margin both rank fourth out of five. Nike trades at 18.4 times its earnings over its latest four fiscal quarters, compared with 15.0 times for Tapestry (TPR). Over each company's latest four quarters, Nike's revenue fell 1.2%, while Tapestry's revenue grew 14.2%.

Nike also keeps far less of each sale as profit. The company posted an 8.2% operating margin, well below the 23.9% margin at Tapestry. Only Ralph Lauren (RL) costs more than Nike and grows faster, trading at 23.4 times earnings alongside a 14.7% increase in revenue. Where Nike's Sales Grow And Where They Fall

Nike is primarily a shoe company, with footwear bringing in $30.5 billion of its $46.4 billion in revenue for fiscal 2026. Its largest positions include RTX Corp (NYSE:RTX) at 9.05%, GE Aerospace (NYSE:GE) at 9.04%, and Boeing Co (NYSE:BA) at 8.83%. The fund holds 68 securities. It was launched in 2005. Invesco Aerospace & Defense ETF has paid $0.66 per share over the trailing 12 months, which, on its recent ~$155.3 share price, works out to a 0.4% yield.

State Street SPDR S&P Aerospace & Defense ETF provides exposure to 50 holdings through a modified equal-weight approach, which reduces the influence of the largest defense contractors. Its top holdings include Honeywell Aerospace Inc (NASDAQ:HONA) at 3.33%, Lockheed Martin Corp (NYSE:LMT) at 3.15%, and Transdigm Group Inc (NYSE:TDG) at 3.12%. It was launched in 2011. Which looks like the better buy

When comparing the Invesco Aerospace & Defense ETF (PPA) and the State Street SPDR S&P Aerospace & Defense ETF (XAR), investors should consider several key factors. Let's see what they tell us about each fund.

First, we should examine each fund's strategy. Let's take PPA first. It employs a market cap weighting model. As a result, its top 15 holdings comprise about 68% of its total assets. XAR, by contrast, has a modified equal-weighted strategy. Therefore, smaller, high-growth stocks can impact the fund's performance more than in the case of PPA.

Two other important factors are historical performance and income potential. Over the last five years, XAR has generated a total return of 112%, equating to a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 16.2%. PPA, meanwhile, has delivered an 81% total return, with a 12.6% CAGR. Both funds pay modest dividends. PPA has a dividend yield of 0.4%, while XAR's is 0.2%.

One final factor to weigh is cost. XAR has the lower expense ratio of 0.35%, while PPA's is 0.58%. To put that in context, if a person were to buy $10,000 of each fund, they should expect to pay $35 in annual fees for their XAR shares but $58 in annual fees for their PPA shares.

In summary, PPA and XAR are both ETFs focused on aerospace stocks, but they are structured differently and differ in several key respects. For many investors, XAR will be the more appealing of the two funds. It has a lower expense ratio and has performed better historically. It also offers greater diversification due to its weighting strategy.
